s09.slug: THURSDAY · 6:55 AM · THE SILVERADO, ROUTE 60 SOUTH → PITTSBURGH INTERNATIONAL
body: Christmas Eve starts black and clear over Beaver County, the stars still out over the hills and the road dry for the first time since Saturday, white with salt in the headlights. Frank had them out of the driveway at a quarter past six. The heater is still making up its mind. On the bench seat, folded square in the place where a third person would sit, is the Browns parka — orange and brown, older than Gina, the cuff mended with electrical tape. Frank carried it out of the garage in the dark and put it there before Jack came out of the house with the thermos.

KDKA is on low: the airport weather, the Parkway, a man who wants them to know about a mattress sale on the twenty-sixth. A few minutes past seven the newsman stops reading traffic. The Senate, he says, has passed the health-care bill, sixty to thirty-nine, in a vote taken at seven o’clock this morning — the first time the Senate has voted on Christmas Eve since 1895 — with the Vice President in the chair and not one Republican for it.
Frank turns it up a notch and listens to the end of it. When the airport weather comes back he turns it down.
“Merry Christmas,” Frank says.

“They bought Nebraska,” Jack says. “Medicaid for one state, forever, so one senator would vote yes. The House put Stupak’s language in so tax money doesn’t pay for abortions, and the Senate wrote something that sounds like Stupak and isn’t. They’ll find a way to pay for it. They always find a way.”
Frank drives. Off to the left, behind the hills, the sky has started to go gray.

“Your grandmother’s hand,” he says. “Medicare. And it still sent a bill with a comma in it. It’s on the kitchen table, under your mother’s list.” He checks the mirror. “Stupak’s a good man. They’ll beat him for it.” A salt truck, and Frank goes around it on the left with no blinker, there being no blinker on that side. “Nebraska gets something. The insurance guys get something. Some guy laid off in Lordstown whose kid gets sick gets something.” He settles back into the right lane. “Everybody gets something.”
Jack has an answer for that, and the answer to the answer, and drinks his coffee instead.

At ten after eight the sun is up pink over the long-term lots and Pittsburgh International is full of people trying to get somewhere by tonight. Frank took the parka off the seat when they parked and carried it in over his arm. Theo comes down the escalator into baggage claim in the camel coat with a garment bag over one shoulder and a Neiman Marcus bag in the other hand, unshaven, the red-eye gray under both eyes and in the hair he hasn’t done anything about. He sees them at the bottom and puts on charming somewhere around the middle of the escalator.
Frank hands him the parka without a word. Theo sets the Neiman Marcus bag down on the tile and puts the parka on over the camel coat without one, and picks the bag back up.

In the truck Theo gets in the middle, with the garment bag laid across his knees and Jack’s, and by the time they’re down out of the parking garage he’s talking. He saw *Avatar* three times in four days, in IMAX, in the glasses. “Once for the story. Twice for the floating mountains. You have to see the mountains twice or they don’t count.” His mother’s life coach has acquired a life coach, and the two of them came to dinner on Sunday and disagreed about his mother in front of her.

body.text: “I had that ready Monday,” he tells Jack. “You ruined it. I’ve carried it across the country.”

body: Christmas Eve at his father’s in Brentwood would have been a caterer and a tree delivered already decorated, in a color the decorator called *oyster*.
“Oyster,” Frank says.
“A kind of beige, sir. With ambitions.”
Jack watches him work: the timing, the detail stacked on detail, every line built for an audience Theo believes hasn’t been told how this ends. Jack has been told. He lets him do it anyway.
At the merge onto Route 60 Theo runs out, or lets himself run out, and looks through the windshield at the hills going by with the old snow on them.
“How’s Ohio?”
“Cold.”
“And otherwise?”

choices.key: Driving Theo home from the airport on Christmas Eve morning, he asked how Ohio was, otherwise. You told him it’s Ohio.
response: “Otherwise it’s Ohio.”

Theo looks out at the fields — white, the fences drawn across them in black, a barn with a lit star on its peak in the daylight — and doesn’t push, and Jack doesn’t give, and that rides along with them to the state line like a fourth passenger with its knees up.

They’re on Glenwood at twenty to ten. Nonna is asleep in her chair by the front window with the lamp still on in the daylight and her beads stopped in her lap, under Theo’s gray cashmere, tucked in at both sides. Theo stops in the doorway in the parka with the Neiman Marcus bag hanging from his hand and looks at that, and his face, looking, is about ten years old. He goes to wash his hands for the fish.

choices.key: Driving Theo home from the airport on Christmas Eve morning, he asked how Ohio was, otherwise. You asked him how the hills were.
response: “How were the hills?”
Theo goes very still in the middle of the seat, in the parka, with the garment bag across his knees. He stays that way through an exit and most of an overpass.
“What hills?” Frank says.
“Beverly, sir,” Theo says. “Overrated.” And he turns his head and looks at Jack with nothing on his face but the red-eye, and Jack looks back at him until Theo faces front again.

choices.key: Driving Theo home from the airport on Christmas Eve morning, he asked how Ohio was, otherwise. You told him: later.
response: “Later.”
Theo looks at him. A mile goes by: a billboard for a personal-injury lawyer with snow along its top edge, a church with its Nativity lit up in broad daylight, a Sheetz.
“Later,” Theo says.
Frank turns the radio up.

Theo stops in the doorway in the parka with the Neiman Marcus bag hanging from his hand and looks at that, and his face, looking, is about ten years old. He goes to wash his hands for the fish.

body: By four the kitchen windows have steamed over from the inside, and the radio on top of the refrigerator — Nonna’s, tuned since before Jack was born to the AM station out of Warren that plays the Italian Christmas records all day on the twenty-fourth — has come around to the donkey.

The baccalà is up out of the basement sink at last and simmering in Ma’s tomatoes with the olives. The clams wait in a colander for the linguine. On the back of the counter, coiled in a Pyrex dish under foil where Frank won’t have to look at it, is the eel — *capitone*, which Nonna has put on this table every Christmas Eve since 1951 and which Frank has refused every Christmas Eve since he married in. He has been out in the garage since three.

Theo is at the sink in the ST. BRIGID’S FISH FRY 2006 apron with the sleeves of a navy sweater shoved up past his elbows, cleaning squid. Nonna is directing from her chair, which Frank carried into the kitchen doorway for her after lunch, with Theo’s gray throw over her knees and her beads in her left hand, and she is not satisfied. She says something in Calabrese, at length.
“She says you hold it like a baby you don’t like,” Gina says from the table, where she has her hands in the dough for the bread with the anchovies baked in.

“I hold all babies like this,” Theo says. “Ask my sister.” He turns the squid over, draws the quill out of it, clear as a strip of cellophane, and holds it up toward the doorway for inspection. Nonna allows it with her chin.

He has been learning the rules since ten, with two hours off for Trumbull, and has come back from it needing to be useful. Seven fishes: never six, never eight. No meat in the house till midnight, not even for the dog — there is no dog; Nonna is speaking generally. The anchovies in the bread count as a fish, whatever Danny used to say about it. You don’t sit down at the table before Nonna sits. And the eel isn’t one of the seven. Gina, asked to translate why, consulted Nonna and came back with it: “It’s a penance. For the men.”

Rosie is kneeling on a chair at the counter doing the donkey along with the radio — she has had the donkey’s part by heart since she was four — and she has been teaching it to Theo, who learns it the way he learns everything, too fast and with questions. “Is he an Italian donkey?” “He’s from *Italy*,” Rosie says, appalled. Theo does the donkey. He does it well. Gina puts her forehead down on the floured table. “I’m going to die in this kitchen,” she says into the dough. “They’re going to find me in the bread.”

body.text: Jack has been on the smelts since they got back from Trumbull — the head off, the belly opened with a thumb, the spine out in one pull, a mixing bowl of them silver on the counter beside him — and when the squid are done there are the shrimp, and after the shrimp whatever Ma points at.
When Jack brings his bowl to the sink, Theo shifts over to give him the faucet. One look across it, and back to the squid.

body: At four Nonna wants the Pope, and Ma turns the little set at the end of the counter to EWTN with a wet hand. Rome is six hours ahead and lit gold: St. Peter’s at ten at night, the nave full to the doors, the procession coming up the middle between the wooden barriers, the cameras following the white of him, the commentator murmuring about the choir. Jack has sat down across from Gina with a squid in one hand and the knife in the other to watch him come.

A woman in the crowd goes over the barrier. It’s fast — the camera barely has her: a lunge, a scrum, the white figure dropping out of the frame and men in black closing over the place where he was. Jack is on his feet. The chair goes over behind him. Nonna’s beads come up in her fist. Ma’s hand goes to her mouth. The commentator says *Oh — oh, dear*, and then can’t find anything else to say, and the picture is the backs of men’s heads and a candle tipping in somebody’s hand.
And Theo, at the sink, isn’t watching the television. He’s watching Jack.

They have him up. The white figure is standing among the cardinals with somebody’s hand at his elbow, and they start him walking, and the procession goes on up the nave toward the altar with the choir still singing. An old cardinal went down too, the commentator says, finding his voice; they’re seeing to him. The Mass begins.
Jack is still standing there with the squid. From her chair at the counter Rosie says, small, “Is he okay?” “He’s up,” Ma says. “Look. He’s up.” Nonna crosses herself with the beads, twice.
Inside a minute the phone buzzes in his back pocket.

body.text: He’s in my missal. I’m being nice to him. —L.

response.text: He always does. That’s the job. —L.

response: By half past the squid are done and in their flour, and Ma has stopped looking up at the television every two minutes, and in Rome the old man is at the altar saying the Mass he came to say. Rosie has the donkey going again without the radio. At 4:52 the phone goes in his pocket.

s12.slug: THURSDAY · 6:40 PM · THE FRONT ROOM — LA VIGILIA
body: The dining table has been carried into the front room, where there’s space for it, with the card table butted onto the end under the same white cloth, and Nonna is at the head in her own chair with the tree lit behind her and the cashmere over her knees. At twenty to seven Ma comes in from the kitchen with the bread and sees what Nonna has done.

Nonna set it while Ma was down in the basement: at her right hand, where it has always been, a plate, a glass, and the napkin ring from his First Communion, silver plate gone soft at the edges, *D.F.C. 1995*, with one of the good napkins drawn through it.

Ma stops with the bread. Down at the other end of the table Frank has seen it too, and the two of them look at each other the length of the cloth, and Ma puts the bread down beside it and goes back for the clams.

Theo, coming in behind her with the baccalà, sees it too. He sets the baccalà down, and goes out to the garage, and comes back with a folding chair with a Local 1112 sticker on the back, and opens it at the corner by Rosie.

“Phones,” Ma says, and holds out the bread basket — the second one, the empty one, lined with a dish towel — at the end of the sideboard. Gina drops hers in with a sigh that goes on past the phone. Theo lays his iPhone in on top of it gently, a coat left at a coat check. Jack puts the RAZR in last, shut, and Ma sets the basket on the sideboard by the window and turns her back on it.
When Nonna is in and settled, Theo half rises off the folding chair. “I’m the guest —”
“You’re not company,” Frank says. “Rosie says it.”
Theo sits back down.

Rosie stands up on her chair rung to be taller and folds her hands under her chin and does the regular grace first, all of it, fast, the way they say it at school, and then keeps going. Thank you for the fish, even the eel. And for Jack being home from California, and for Theo coming from California too. And for the baby in New Orleans. And for Danny, and that he gets to have Christmas where he is. And Nonna’s hand, that it gets better. And Theo’s mom, who has a coach. And the Browns. And Denver, her buffalo, who is under the tree and can’t come to the table. “And the baby in New Orleans,” she says, “again, because she’s new. Through Christ our Lord.”
“Amen,” says the table, and Theo a syllable behind it.

Ma is crying, which she does every year at about this point, and Frank passes his handkerchief up the table to her hand over hand, the same as every year. By the amen the clams have gone cold in their shells.

The fish come around one after another. The smelts, fried crisp enough to eat heads and all; Rosie eats only the tails. The baccalà in its tomatoes, which Nonna tastes and sends a word down the table about, and Ma says, “I know, Ma. I know.” The white fish, which Gina says is whiting and Frank says is whatever was on sale. Theo eats everything. When the linguine comes he reaches for the grated cheese, and Nonna says “*No!*” from the head of the table loud enough to stop Rosie chewing.
“No cheese on fish,” Gina says. “She says in Calabria they’d run you out of town.”
“I withdraw the cheese,” Theo says, and puts it down very carefully, and Nonna looks at him with real affection for the first time since the squid.

The eel has been on the table since grace, fried in rounds in its Pyrex near Frank’s elbow — Nonna had it brought out first, so the men couldn’t hide behind anything — and through the smelts and the baccalà it hasn’t been touched. Frank has moved his water glass to the far side of his plate to be farther from it. At the linguine Nonna runs out of patience. She puts a round on Jack’s plate with her left hand, and one on Theo’s.
Frank takes out his wallet and lays a five on the cloth beside the baccalà.
“First one of you eats that,” he says. “Twenty-four years I never paid out.”

response: He eats it in two bites before he can think about it. It’s rich, oily, sweet under the crisp, and it tastes like a river. Frank looks at him over the baccalà, and pushes the five across it with one finger. “Your brother never would.”
Theo eats his after, slowly, with his eyes shut, explaining it to the table as he goes. There’s no money in it for him. Nonna pats the cloth beside her plate for both of them.

choices.text: “Theo’ll eat mine. He’s from Los Angeles; he eats anything with a story.”
response: Theo eats his own, and then Jack’s, and gives a speech in between about courage and the Romans and an eel he once declined in Kyoto, and at the end of it he asks Nonna, through Gina, for the story.

Nonna gives him one. The eel is the snake from the garden. On Christmas Eve you eat him, so he can’t make trouble in the new year. He swam to Calabria to get away, and her own mother caught him in the river with her hands, in 1931 — “She’s making this up,” Gina says. “*Zitta*,” says Nonna. Frank pays Theo the five.

He forks his round onto Nonna’s plate. She eats it with great satisfaction, in two bites, and says something about Calabria that makes Ma put her napkin over her mouth. “Translate,” Theo says. “No,” says Gina.
Theo eats his own with his eyes shut, explaining it to the table as he goes, and Frank pays him the five.

s12a.slug: THURSDAY · 6:58 PM · THE FRONT ROOM — LA VIGILIA
body: At two minutes to seven, with the linguine going around, the basket on the sideboard buzzes. The RAZR rattles against Theo’s iPhone under the dish towel like something trying to get out.
Rosie is nearest. She’s off her chair before anybody: “*Jack!* Your phone!” — and has it out of the basket in her fist, shut, the little outer screen lit up blue with its envelope —

And Theo is there before she can get it open. He’s out of the folding chair and has the RAZR out of her hand, shut, without any hurry about it, the way you’d take the scissors from a kid who’s only holding them, and he passes it down the table to Jack face-down, without looking at it.
“Yours.”
Jack puts it in his pocket. His ears are hot.
“*Basket*,” Ma says.
He takes it back out and puts it in the basket. Theo is already back on the folding chair, asking Nonna for the bread. Gina has become very interested in a clam.

body.text: Across the table, past Danny’s glass, Theo’s eyes come up and meet his and go back to the bread.

body: The linguine goes, and the shrimp, and the anchovy bread, the seventh. There are the honey cookies Ma and Gina fried Sunday night, and coffee. Frank undoes the top button of his good pants and announces it. The tree lights blink in the black of the front window.
At five to eight Jack is at the sideboard.
“Ma. The levee. I said I’d call.”
Ma looks at him from her end of the table with the coffee pot in her hand.
“Is that the girl?”
“It’s Lena.”
She holds the look one more second. “Take it,” she says. “Tell her Merry Christmas from the Costigans.”
He has the phone out of the basket when the table shouts it — *MERRY CHRISTMAS* — at it, before he’s even dialed, Rosie loudest, Frank with his hands cupped.
From the head of the table Nonna lifts the beads: “*La suora!*”
“Tell her I ate an eel,” Theo says, loudly, to his back.
He goes out through the kitchen, past the pots soaking in the sink, and holds the side door so it won’t bang,, and lets it close on the noise of all of them.
